title: While Shepherds Watched Their Flocks
description: Nahum Tate's Christmas hymn to the tune Winchester Old, in the four parts W. H. Monk wrote for Hymns Ancient and Modern, arranged for 2 to 4 singers: all six verses, as the book prints them, at a steady walk. The tune moves mostly by step in short lines, from the shepherds on the ground to the angels' "All glory be to God on high".

credits.words: Nahum Tate (Supplement to the New Version of the Psalms, 1700)
credits.tune: "Winchester Old", from Thomas Este's The Whole Booke of Psalmes (1592)
credits.arrangement: W. H. Monk's four parts (Hymns Ancient and Modern, 1861, as revised in 1875), adapted by Stackapella

licence.words: public domain: Nahum Tate died 1715; the words first appeared in the Supplement to the New Version of the Psalms by Tate and Nicholas Brady (1700 by the Psalter Hymnal Handbook, 1702 by Julian's Dictionary of Hymnology, both quoted at hymnary.org), in six stanzas; all six sung here as Hymns Ancient and Modern (Revised Edition, 1875), No. 62, prints them, with its spellings ("watch'd", "display'd", "wrapp'd", "Appear'd", "Address'd", "Heav'n"), its capitals ("Angel", "Angels", "Who") and its quotation marks; the small capitals of LORD, CHRIST and GOD written as Lord, Christ and God. "heavenly" (verse 4) is sung in two syllables, "heav-" on the dotted note and "enly" on the crotchet, as the metre needs; "Saviour" (verse 3) in two. The first edition (1861), No. 44, differs only in spelling and in verse 6: "watched", "angel", "displayed", "wrapped", "Appeared", "angels", "Addressed", "And in the earth be peace" (1875: "to the earth"), "Good-will henceforth from Heaven to men" and a closing "Amen"
licence.tune: public domain: "Winchester Old", an anonymous psalm tune first printed in Thomas Este's The Whole Booke of Psalmes (London, 1592); Hymns Ancient and Modern names no composer: its 1861 Index of Tunes gives the source as "Este" and its 1875 index as "Este's Psalter". The tune is sung here as the 1875 book prints it, note for note the same as in 1861
licence.arrangement: W. H. Monk's four parts for Hymns Ancient and Modern (Monk died 1889; public domain), signed "W. H. Monk" under "Harmonized or Arranged by" in the first edition's Index of Tunes (1861, p. xv, "Winchester, Old ... Este ... W. H. Monk ... 44, 130, 157") and printed, revised in six places, in the Revised Edition of 1875, whose music Monk also edited (its index names no harmonizer). Taken from the 1875 page part for part, in its key, with the lower parts revoiced for 2 to 4 beginners so the duet and trio keep each strong beat's third: on "by" (line 1, the sixth note) the alto holds D4 (Monk F4), doubling his tenor, so the B-flat chord keeps its third at 2 and 3 singers; on "on" (line 2, the fourth note) the alto sings E4 and the tenor C4 (Monk G4 and D4), so his G with the tune's suspended C becomes C over G, its third in the alto, before his G chord; on "the" (the next note) the alto sings D4 (Monk G4), stepping E4, D4, E4 into the cadence, and doubles his tenor's D4; on "of" (line 3, the fourth note) the alto sings D4 (Monk F4) and the bass B-flat 2, Monk's own note there in 1861 (his 1875 D3 would move in octaves with the alto); on the last note of each verse the alto sings A3 under the tune's low F4 (Monk C4, a bare fourth under it) and the tenor F3 in unison with the bass (Monk A3), so the last chord has no fifth, as in our O Come, O Come, Emmanuel. Breaths written in for beginners: lines 1 and 3 end on a minim straight into the next line's pickup, so the minim gives up half a beat and the pickup starts a quarter beat late, in every part; lines 2 and 4 end on a dotted semibreve that gives up three quarters of a beat, except the song's last. The pickup keeps Monk's C4 under the tune's F4, a bare fourth on the weak beat before each verse, and the crotchet on "gel" (line 3) his F4 under C5, a passing chord on a weak half beat. Also accepted: in line 3 the bass sings F3, B-flat 2, F3 ("of" and on), two leaps over a fourth in one line, Monk's own 1861 bass at "of", kept because every other note there made octaves with the alto or left the duet without its third. The Amen is left out. Everything else is Monk's 1875 notes. The 1861 first edition differs from the 1875 page in six places, all in the lower parts: on "herds" (line 1) the alto repeats F4 and the bass moves to A2 at the middle of the dotted note, where 1875 holds F with the tune; on "the" before "ground" the alto, tenor and bass sing D4, G3 and G2 (1875: G4, D4, G3); on "ground" the tenor sings G3 (1875: C4); on "The" (line 3) the tenor A3 (1875: C4); on "An-" the bass B-flat 2 (1875: B-flat 3, in unison with the tenor); on "of" the tenor D4 and bass B-flat 2 (1875: B-flat 3 and D3)
licence.source: Hymns Ancient and Modern for use in the Services of the Church, with Accompanying Tunes, compiled and arranged under the musical editorship of William Henry Monk (London: printed by William Clowes and Sons), the Revised Edition of 1875 in a later printing (the Princeton Theological Seminary copy, catalogued 1875, includes the 1889 Supplement, hymns up to 638), No. 62, "Christmas", headed "Winchester Old, C.M." with minim = 112, p. 80, in F major (one flat), barred in four minims with a one-minim pickup to each line, written here in crotchets (4/4) in its printed key, F; the music and words read at archive.org/details/hymnsanci00chur/page/n115, its first-lines index (p. xxxi, "While shepherds ... 62 ... Winchester Old. C.M. ... Este's Psalter") at n30; compared with the first edition with tunes (London: Novello and Co., 1861), No. 44, in F, read from the University of Toronto copy at archive.org/details/hymnsancientmode00unse/page/n79, its Index of Tunes (p. xv) at n21. The 1875 page notes "44 Orig. Ed." "heavenly" in verse 4 is sung in two syllables and shown as "heav'n-ly", as the book itself writes "Heav'n" in verse 6.
